extracted.intended_audience: law students, practitioners, claimant advocates and policy analysts dealing with Canadian unemployment insurance appeals and administrative law
extracted.subtask_short: federal court review of UI appeals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for appeals and judicial review of Canadian unemployment insurance decisions (Boards of referees, Umpires, UIC) including procedural rules, remedies, jurisdictional allocation between Trial and Appeal Divisions, and standards for regulation validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay of proceedings for premiums/insurable employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions relating to premiums and insurable employment must be referred to the Minister of National Revenue under sec. 105 of the Act; the Umpire must stay the appeal proceedings until the Minister has reached a decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matters within the Minister's exclusive province (premiums/insurable employment) are not to be decided by appeals involving benefits; the appeal process should be suspended pending the Minister's determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Umpire's discretion to shorten or simplify procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Under sec. 93(1) of the Act, the Umpire may shorten and simplify the examination procedure as he thinks fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examination broadly follows court-like processes (statements, cross-examination, summing-up), but the Umpire has express statutory discretion to simplify or abbreviate procedural steps when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory procedural rules for reimbursement and privilege
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific statutory rules exist for reimbursement of persons the Umpire requests to appear (sec. 101 and reg. 185(5)) and for a privilege granted to anyone who provides evidence necessary to settle the dispute (sec. 115).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are among the few procedural matters governed by statute; other procedural aspects remain governed by the Umpire's discretion. The text also discusses sec. 114 and the unclear scope of confidentiality vis-à-vis disclosure before the Umpire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Umpire's decision must be in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reg. 186(1) states that the Umpire's decision shall be in writing; Umpires write their decisions in the usual judicial style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, decisions are drafted, authenticated, filed in quadruplicate and distributed; historically it took an average of five weeks and two days to write and forward a decision in the sample period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible dispositions of Umpire decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: For each question raised by an appeal, the Umpire may uphold, rescind, amend the decision of the Board of referees, or send the case back to the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics are kept on outcomes (upheld/rescinded) but other dispositions (amended/sent back) also occur; sample frequencies are provided to illustrate practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on Umpire's power to order write-off of recoverable sums
rubrics_metrics.description: The Umpire can no more rule on the writing-off under reg. 175 of money recoverable from a claimant under overpayments than can the Board of referees; this is a prerogative of the UIC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite the formal limit, Umpires often 'urge' the UIC to write off sums, stressing factors such as the size relative to claimant resources, technical errors by the UIC, long delays in detection, and absence of fraudulent intent. Examples in sample decisions show Umpires recommending write-off in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of rescission on claimant's rights (retroactivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Umpire rescinds a Board decision in the claimant's favour, the claimant's rights are reinstated with effect from the date of the initial decision which had been upheld by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of procedural delays (average of 36 weeks from appeal to notification), reinstatement is retroactive but may not mitigate interim financial hardship; timeliness of the appeal process is therefore a substantive concern for income security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspensive effect of UIC appeals and timing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions recognize the suspensive effect of appeals filed by the UIC only if they are filed within 21 days of the Board of referees' decision and are based either on the claimant's disentitlement under sec. 44 or on the allegation that the Board failed to take a provision of the Act or Regulations into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If these conditions are not met, payments made under Board decisions are treated as duly paid; timing and stated grounds are determinative of suspensive effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for leave to appeal to the Umpire ('principle of importance' / 'special circumstances')
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimant may be denied leave to appeal to the Umpire if no 'principle of importance' is involved and there are no 'special circumstances' justifying the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Umpire finds that the appellant has presented new facts, he may send the case back to the Board for full review. Often, a request for re-examination under sec. 102 is more appropriate than an application for leave to appeal; misuse of procedure to seek a de facto re-opening delays resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for sending a case back to the Board of referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Common reasons include the appearance of new facts submitted after the Board's decision, the Board's failure to rule on questions raised in submissions, and inadequacy of evidence obtained by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal to the Umpire is 'useful' only when the UIC and Board refuse to recognize that facts contain new elements; otherwise sec. 102 re-examination is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability of decisions based on incomplete fact-finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions reached on representations made in the absence of the claimant, where the claimant did not attend, because of language problems, or because hearings were held too far away, are more vulnerable to criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequacy of evidence and opportunity to be heard are factual predicates for reliable Board decisions; absence of the primary fact-witness undermines decision robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Umpire's usual practice to send files back rather than withhold decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Although sec. 99 authorizes the Umpire to withhold his decision until the Board has reconsidered, the normal procedure is for the Umpire to send the file back to the Board of referees to reach a definitive decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The file may later return to the Umpire only after another appeal by the claimant against the Board's second decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of administrative decisions for Federal Court jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Court Act (secs. 18 and 28) distinguishes decisions into 'judicial or quasi-judicial' and 'purely administrative' (the latter described as 'decisions or orders of an administrative nature not required by law to be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This initial classification is vague but determines whether the Trial Division or the Appeal Division reviews the decision. Proper classification is therefore a key procedural step for litigants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventive vs remedial review (choice of remedy and division)
rubrics_metrics.description: A second criterion distinguishes 'preventive' review (traditional remedies like prohibition or mandamus before the Trial Division) from 'remedial' or a posteriori review (application to review and set aside) before the Appeal Division under sec. 28(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Appeal Division's remedial review is broader and may include directing corrective measures (sec. 52(d)). The chosen remedy affects both immediate relief and subsequent appeal routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of remedy/division allocation on appeal opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions before the Trial Division may be appealed to the Court of Appeal (sec. 27(1)) and possibly to the Supreme Court (sec. 31(1)), but appeals from the Appeal Division require leave to proceed to the Supreme Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The allocation affects strategic litigation choices: which remedy to pursue, the prospects of further appeal, and whether the case is fit for the Court of Appeal or Trial Division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical difficulty in recourse to the Federal Court
rubrics_metrics.description: Recourse to the Federal Court is extremely technical for the appellant, involving difficult problems with regard to the choice of remedy and the choice of court; the Federal Court Act's substantive ambiguities and archaic wording exacerbate this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Litigants must carefully select the appropriate remedy and forum; misfiling in the wrong division can lead to dismissal without a hearing on the merits (illustrated by Kraynick and Mahaffey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chairman's refusal to grant leave is a 'decision or order' under sec. 28(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The refusal of leave to appeal by the chairman of a Board of referees constitutes a 'decision or order' within the meaning of sec. 28(1), given its legal effect of settling the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such matters should be brought before the Federal Court of Appeal rather than the Trial Division; sec. 102's lack of authorization for the chairman to amend his own decision makes the chairman's refusal effectively final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Court intervention in Umpire decisions (sec. 100)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Umpire decisions were presented as final, the Unemployment Insurance Act expressly provides for Federal Court intervention (sec. 100); historically, these interventions have been handled by the Appeal Division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most judicial review of Umpires' decisions has been by the Court of Appeal, reflecting the remedial-review function and avoiding Trial Division judges reviewing decisions made in their capacity as Umpires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground for setting aside decisions: error in law
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications to review and set aside Umpire (and other administrative) decisions have been brought on the ground that the decision 'erred in law'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful appeals to set aside an Umpire's decision typically require establishing legal error rather than mere disagreement with factual findings (examples include Paulsen and McPherson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for upholding regulatory validity (interconnection test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulation (e.g., reg. 145(9)) is valid where it 'subordinates proof of the fulfilment of the conditions specified by the Act to proof of a fact which is so interconnected with the fulfilment of these conditions that it is impossible to conceive of the legal conditions being fulfilled without the existence of the fact required by the regulation'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory requirements like proving 'reasonable and customary efforts' to obtain employment must be assessed 'in concreto' — efforts are 'reasonable in the circumstances'; fixed, pre-established numeric standards used by UIC could be contested by claimants relying on this case law (Ricard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations must not unlawfully limit delegated powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory provisions that in substance impose unwarranted self-imposed limitations on the delegation of power (e.g., fixing a maximum antedating period) can be struck down as beyond the scope of the enabling provision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will examine whether a regulation is a permissible condition or an improper limitation on statutory authority (example: Attorney General v. the Umpire striking down subsec. (2) and (3) of reg. 150).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical emphasis of Federal Court review: legality of regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The experience to date indicates that the Federal Court's major area of intervention with regard to unemployment insurance will be in the review of the legality of regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While individual decisions are reviewable, precedent shows regulatory challenges (validity, scope) are a central focus of federal judicial review in this field.
